entities.name: Maximilian of Lorch
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saint Maximilian of Lorch, also known as Maximilian of Celeia, stands as a pivotal figure in the early Christianization of the Roman province of Noricum, a region encompassing modern-day Austria and Slovenia. His martyrdom, traditionally dated to October 12, 284 (though some sources suggest 288), under the reign of Emperor Numerian (or later Diocletian), solidified his status as one of the most venerated early Christian bishops and missionaries in the Eastern Alps. His life and death are emblematic of the challenges faced by nascent Christian communities in the Roman Empire, particularly during periods of imperial persecution, establishing a local foundation for Christian identity that would endure for centuries.

Maximilian's ministry reportedly centered in Lauriacum (modern Lorch, near Enns, Austria), a significant Roman legionary camp and administrative center. As bishop, he was instrumental in consolidating Christian communities that had begun to emerge in the 3rd century, often operating in a hostile environment characterized by official Roman polytheism and intermittent persecution. The narrative of his arrest typically describes his refusal to renounce his faith, leading to his execution by beheading. While specific details of his episcopacy and the exact circumstances of his death are largely drawn from later hagiographical traditions, these accounts underscore the unwavering commitment expected of Christian leaders during the age of martyrs and provide insight into the spread of the new religion through personal sacrifice.
